intro: Open any Bible and you hold the end of a very long chain. Someone wrote a letter to a house church in Rome around 57 CE. Someone copied it, and someone copied the copy. Councils and bishops argued over which books belonged. Scribes in the desert and in monasteries preserved the text. Scholars in Bethlehem, Oxford, Worms and London put it into Latin and then English, some of them at the cost of their lives. This unit follows that chain from Paul's pen to the copy on your desk.

The first chapter reads two of Paul's letters closely, Galatians and Romans. They are short, difficult and enormously influential: Augustine, Luther and Wesley each traced a turning point in their lives to Romans, and readers still argue over what Paul meant by faith, law and grace, and over what he said about women, slavery and the state. You will learn to read a letter as a whole, in its occasion, and to say which reading of it belongs to which tradition.

The second chapter asks three questions about the Bible as a physical object. Which books belong, and why do Jewish, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles differ? Which wording is oldest, and how do scholars decide when manuscripts disagree? And how does a Hebrew or Greek word become an English one? By the end you will be able to explain a disputed verse, cite the manuscripts and translations behind it, and describe each community's reading fairly, without deciding for anyone which is true.
bigQuestion: How did the Bible reach us in the form we have, and who has had a say in what its words mean?

timeline.t: The Torah is translated into Greek in Alexandria; the Septuagint begins
The Great Isaiah Scroll is copied, later found at Qumran
Paul writes 1 Thessalonians, the earliest surviving Christian document
Paul dictates the letter to the Romans in Corinth
Marcion proposes a Christian scripture without the Old Testament and is expelled
Athanasius's Easter letter lists the 27 books of the New Testament
Jerome finishes the Latin Vulgate from Hebrew and Greek
Wycliffe's followers produce the first complete English Bible
Luther, shaped by Romans, posts the Ninety-five Theses
Tyndale prints the first English New Testament from Greek
The King James Bible is published
The Dead Sea Scrolls are found near Qumran

test.q: Which of Paul's letters was written first, and roughly when?
test.why: 1 Thessalonians, c. 50 CE, is the earliest surviving Christian writing; Romans came about seven years later.

test.q: What did Paul's opponents in Galatia teach, according to his letter?
choices: That Jesus was not the messiah
That Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law
That Paul should go to Spain
test.why: Galatians 5:2–3 and 6:12 show the dispute was over circumcision and the law for Gentiles.

test.q: Why does Paul stress that Abraham believed before he was circumcised?
choices: To show Abraham was a Gentile
To show circumcision was a mistake
To argue that people belong by faith, as Abraham did
To date the book of Genesis
test.why: Galatians 3 and Romans 4 use Genesis 15:6, which comes before Genesis 17, to argue that faith, not the law, made Abraham righteous.

test.q: Which verse in Galatians did abolitionists and advocates of women's equality both cite?
test.why: Galatians 3:28, neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female, has been read as a charter of equality.

test.q: What does Paul conclude about Israel in Romans 11?
choices: That Israel has been replaced by the church
That the gifts and calling of God cannot be taken back
That Gentiles should keep the Torah
That the law was a mistake
test.why: Romans 11:29 says the gifts and calling of God are without repentance; Paul warns Gentiles not to boast against the branches.

test.q: How did the Council of Trent differ from Luther on justification?
choices: Trent taught justification by works alone
Trent taught that justification also makes a person inwardly righteous, with faith working through love
test.why: Luther read justification as God declaring the sinner righteous by faith alone; Trent (1547) taught that it also transforms the person.

test.q: What did E. P. Sanders's Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) argue?
choices: That the Pastoral letters are genuine
That first-century Judaism was based on covenant and grace, not earning salvation
test.why: Sanders's covenantal nomism described Jews keeping the law within a covenant already given by grace, which reshaped readings of Paul.
The Tanakh counts 24 books; Protestant Bibles have 66, Catholic 73, and the New Testament 27.

test.q: Which books are in Catholic Bibles but not in the Tanakh or Protestant Bibles?
test.why: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1–2 Maccabees are deuterocanonical for Catholics and Apocrypha for Protestants.

test.q: What did Marcion's proposed canon contain?
choices: An edited Luke and ten letters of Paul
test.why: Marcion, c. 144 CE, rejected the Old Testament and kept an edited Luke with ten Pauline letters.

test.q: Which manuscript is a complete copy of Isaiah dated c. 125 BCE?
test.why: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran is the best-preserved of the Dead Sea Scrolls.

test.q: What rule do textual critics follow when one reading is rougher than another?
choices: Prefer the harder reading, since scribes smoothed texts
test.why: Scribes tended to remove difficulties, so the harder reading is more likely the earlier one.

test.q: What did Jerome produce between c. 382 and 405?
test.why: Jerome translated the Bible into Latin from Hebrew and Greek; his version became the Vulgate.

test.q: Which English translator worked from Erasmus's Greek New Testament and was executed in 1536?
test.why: Tyndale printed his New Testament in 1526 and was strangled and burned near Brussels in 1536.

test.q: Why does the King James Version read a virgin at Isaiah 7:14 while the 1917 JPS reads the young woman?
choices: The King James follows the Septuagint's Greek; the JPS renders the Hebrew almah
The JPS translators removed the prophecy
The King James translators misread the Hebrew letters
test.why: Parthenos in the Septuagint, followed by the Vulgate and the King James, usually means virgin; the Hebrew almah means a young woman.

write.prompt: Did Paul think the law of Moses still mattered for the people of God? Argue from the text. Cite Galatians 3:28, Galatians 5:14 and Romans 11:18, or two of these plus one passage of your choice. Explain what each passage says in its place in the letter, then describe how Luther, the New Perspective and at least one Jewish reader have read it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you use, and say which translation you are quoting.
Attribute every reading to its reader or tradition: Luther read…, Sanders argued…, Jewish tradition holds….
Read each passage in its occasion. Say who Paul was writing to and what problem he was answering.
Compare readings; do not judge which tradition is right.
Use the unit's terms: occasion, works of the law, justified, grace, canon.
